claim: PI3K signalling promotes the transition from naïve endoderm precursors into committed anterior endoderm
source: We found that PI3K signalling promotes the transition from naïve endoderm precursors into committed anterior endoderm.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing that PI3K inhibition blocks anterior endoderm formation.

claim: PI3K promoted commitment via an atypical activity that delimited epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)
source: PI3K promoted commitment via an atypical activity that delimited epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT).
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that PI3K inhibition leads to loss of epithelial markers and increased EMT markers (Figure 4A,B).

claim: Akt1 transduced PI3K activity via modifications to the extracellular matrix (ECM)
source: Akt1 transduced this activity via modifications to the extracellular matrix (ECM) and appropriate ECM could itself induce anterior endodermal identity in the absence of PI3K signalling.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that ECM produced under normal conditions (ECM1) can rescue anterior endoderm formation in the presence of PI3K inhibitor (Figure 6B).

claim: Appropriate ECM could itself induce anterior endodermal identity in the absence of PI3K signalling
source: Akt1 transduced this activity via modifications to the extracellular matrix (ECM) and appropriate ECM could itself induce anterior endodermal identity in the absence of PI3K signalling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments where cells plated on ECM1 in the presence of LY (PI3K inhibitor) still form anterior endoderm (Figure 6B).

claim: PI3K/Akt1-modified ECM contained low levels of Fibronectin (Fn1)
source: PI3K/Akt1-modified ECM contained low levels of Fibronectin (Fn1) and we found that Fn1 dose was key to specifying anterior endodermal identity in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS analysis showing Fn1 enrichment in ECM2 (produced with PI3K inhibition) compared to ECM1 (Figure 7A).

claim: Fn1 dose was key to specifying anterior endodermal identity in vivo and in vitro
source: PI3K/Akt1-modified ECM contained low levels of Fibronectin (Fn1) and we found that Fn1 dose was key to specifying anterior endodermal identity in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that exogenous Fn1 blocks anterior endoderm formation (Figure 7C) and Fn1 null embryos show expanded anterior endoderm domain (Figure 8E).

claim: Localized PI3K activity affects ECM composition and ECM in turn patterns the endoderm
source: Thus, localized PI3K activity affects ECM composition and ECM in turn patterns the endoderm.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by multiple experiments showing PI3K-dependent ECM changes and ECM-dependent endoderm patterning.

claim: PI3K inhibition with LY had a specific effect on induction of ADE but not on mesendodermal populations
source: However, while inhibition of different MAPKs (with PD032, SP and SB) also resulted in a dramatic reduction in mesendodermal and pan-endodermal, Hhex−Cxcr4+ (H−C+) populations, only PI3K inhibition with LY had a specific effect on induction of ADE (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 1C showing that LY treatment specifically reduces Hhex+Cxcr4+ (ADE) population while maintaining Hhex-Cxcr4+ (mesendoderm) population.

claim: PI3K inhibition leads to enhanced expression of pan-endodermal markers Sox17, Foxa2 and Gsc
source: We found that the expression of pan-endodermal markers Sox17, Foxa2 and Gsc were enhanced by PI3K inhibition, while induction of all ADE specific gene expression (Hhex, Cer1, Lefty1, Sfrp5 and Fzd5) was repressed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by q-RT-PCR data in Figure 2A demonstrating increased expression of these markers in LY-treated cultures.

claim: PI3K inhibition represses induction of all ADE specific gene expression including Hhex, Cer1, Lefty1, Sfrp5 and Fzd5
source: We found that the expression of pan-endodermal markers Sox17, Foxa2 and Gsc were enhanced by PI3K inhibition, while induction of all ADE specific gene expression (Hhex, Cer1, Lefty1, Sfrp5 and Fzd5) was repressed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by q-RT-PCR data in Figure 2A showing reduced expression of these ADE markers in LY-treated cultures.

claim: pAkt1 was down-regulated as cells enter phase 1 but levels were rapidly restored at day 2 of differentiation
source: pAkt1 was down-regulated just as cells enter phase 1, but levels were rapidly restored at day 2 of differentiation, and maintained throughout the endodermal differentiation (Figure 2C, upper panel).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 2C demonstrating the temporal pattern of Akt1 phosphorylation during differentiation.

claim: LY rapidly suppressed Akt1 phosphorylation
source: LY rapidly suppressed Akt1 phosphorylation and while pAkt1 levels exhibited a slight recovery 6 hr after LY addition, they remained low throughout differentiation (Figure 2C, middle and bottom panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot data in Figure 2C showing loss of pAkt1 signal after LY treatment.

claim: PI3K was essential between days 3 and 5 of differentiation for ADE induction
source: Figure 3A shows the induction of ADE at day 7, in cultures exposed to LY for different periods of time, and demonstrates that PI3K was essential between days 3 and 5 of differentiation.
evidence: This is shown by time course experiments in Figure 3A where LY treatment during days 3-5 blocks ADE formation.

claim: Hhex+ ADE cells were always Gschigh suggesting they arose specifically from the earlier GschighHhex− population
source: We found that Hhex+ ADE cells were always Gschigh suggesting they arose specifically from the earlier GschighHhex− population.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry analysis showing correlation between Gsc expression levels and Hhex expression.

claim: The Gschigh population was diminished in the presence of LY while the Gsclow population was considerably expanded
source: We also found that this Gschigh population was diminished in the presence of LY while the Gsclow population was considerably expanded (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and imaging data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B showing shift in Gsc expression levels with LY treatment.

claim: When LY-treated cells were released from the PI3K block and cultured for an additional 3 days, there was a complete recovery of Hhex induction
source: When LY-treated cells were released from the PI3K block and cultured for an additional 3 days in phase 2 differentiation conditions, we observed a complete recovery of Hhex induction, suggesting that in the absence of PI3K cells fail to progress in differentiation, but they were maintained in a less differentiated endodermal naïve state (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 3B demonstrating rescue of Hhex expression after LY removal.

claim: In the absence of PI3K cells fail to progress in differentiation but are maintained in a less differentiated endodermal naïve state
source: When LY-treated cells were released from the PI3K block and cultured for an additional 3 days in phase 2 differentiation conditions, we observed a complete recovery of Hhex induction, suggesting that in the absence of PI3K cells fail to progress in differentiation, but they were maintained in a less differentiated endodermal naïve state (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the reversibility of the LY phenotype shown in Figure 3B and supported by marker expression analysis.

claim: LY-treated cultures expressed high levels of early primitive streak markers such as Mixl1 and Cdh2 but not mesodermal specific gene expression
source: Alongside the high levels of endodermal markers previously observed (Sox17, Foxa2) in LY-treated cultures, they also showed expression of early primitive streak markers such as Mixl1 and Cdh2, but not mesodermal specific gene expression (Meox1, Meox2, Mesp1, Mesp2, Isl1, Gata1) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by q-RT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing expression patterns of these markers.

claim: 90% of the Gsc+ cells in LY-treated cultures co-expressed Sox17
source: While these cultures expressed high level of PS gene expression, this appears to be predominantly endoderm as 90% of the Gsc+ cells in these LY-treated cultures co-expressed Sox17 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E demonstrating co-expression of these markers.

claim: LY-treated cells do not up-regulate the expression of posterior (Cdx2) or visceral (Hnf4a, Dab2) endoderm markers
source: These cells also do not up-regulate the expression of posterior (Cdx2), or visceral (Hnf4a, Dab2) endoderm markers.
evidence: This is stated based on gene expression analysis, though specific data is referenced as 'data not shown'.

claim: ADE cells progressed efficiently into hepatocyte and Pdx1 positive pancreatic progenitor lineages
source: While ADE cells progressed efficiently into both lineages, LY-treated cells failed to differentiate efficiently (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining for hepatocyte markers (Figure 3C) and pancreatic markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: LY-treated cells failed to differentiate efficiently into hepatocyte or pancreatic progenitors
source: While ADE cells progressed efficiently into both lineages, LY-treated cells failed to differentiate efficiently (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown by reduced expression of differentiation markers in LY-treated cells compared to control ADE (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: When LY-treated naïve cells were returned to normal differentiation for 3 days prior to hepatocyte differentiation, they performed as normal Hhex positive ADE cultures
source: However, when LY-treated naïve cells were returned to normal differentiation for 3 days prior to subjecting them to hepatocyte differentiation, they performed as normal Hhex positive ADE cultures, efficiently generating Hnf4a/AFP positive hepatocyte progenitors (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 3C showing efficient hepatocyte marker expression in recovered cells.

claim: The Gsclow population generated in the presence of LY failed to make cell–cell contacts and no longer maintained epithelial morphology
source: We found that the Gsclow population generated in the presence of LY failed to make cell–cell contacts and no longer maintained the epithelial morphology normally observed at this early stage of endoderm differentiation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,D, bright field).
evidence: This is shown by brightfield microscopy images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,D demonstrating loss of epithelial organization.

claim: Normal up-regulation of E-cadherin was not observed in LY-treated cultures and residual E-cadherin was not localized to cell–cell junctions
source: Importantly, normal up-regulation of E-cadherin was not observed and residual E-cadherin was not localized to cell–cell junctions, while the pro-EMT transcription factor Snai1 was up-regulated (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence (Figure 4A) and q-RT-PCR (Figure 4B) showing altered E-cadherin expression and localization.

claim: The pro-EMT transcription factor Snai1 was up-regulated in LY-treated cultures
source: Importantly, normal up-regulation of E-cadherin was not observed and residual E-cadherin was not localized to cell–cell junctions, while the pro-EMT transcription factor Snai1 was up-regulated (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is shown by q-RT-PCR data in Figure 4B demonstrating increased Snai1 expression with LY treatment.

claim: In the absence of PI3K signalling, naïve endoderm precursor cells remained in an extended EMT-like process instead of forming an organized epithelium
source: These observations indicated that in the absence of PI3K signalling, naïve endoderm precursor cells remained in an extended EMT-like process, instead of forming an organized epithelium.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of loss of epithelial markers, increased EMT markers, and altered morphology in LY-treated cultures.

claim: pAkt1 levels were significantly higher in the Gschigh cells sorted from differentiating ESCs at day 4.5
source: Figure 4C shows that pAkt1 levels were significantly higher in the Gschigh cells sorted from differentiating ESCs at the time at which Gschigh and Gsclow states could first be distinguished (day 4.5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 4C showing differential pAkt1 levels in sorted cell populations.

claim: The GschighpAkt1high population was endodermal (Sox17+) whereas the GsclowpAkt1low population was mesendodermal (Brachyury+)
source: Q-RT-PCR analysis on the different fractions also indicated that the GschighpAkt1high population was endodermal (Sox17+), whereas the GsclowpAkt1low population formed under control conditions was still mesendodermal (Brachyury+) (T+) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown by q-RT-PCR data in Figure 4D demonstrating differential marker expression in sorted populations.

claim: The Gsclow population formed in the presence of LY expressed high levels of Sox17 whereas T expression was reduced
source: The Gsclow population formed in the presence of LY was also distinct from the Gsclow population formed under control conditions. Gsclow-LY treated cells expressed high levels of Sox17 whereas T expression was reduced (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by q-RT-PCR data in Figure 4E showing marker expression in LY-treated Gsclow cells.

claim: Tam stimulated Akt1 activation rescued ADE generation in the presence of LY
source: In this cell line, we found that Tam stimulated Akt1 activation rescued ADE generation in the presence of LY. This ability of pAkt1 to support ADE specification was observed both by flow cytometry (Figure 5A) and by q-RT-PCR (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry (Figure 5A) and q-RT-PCR (Figure 5C) showing restoration of ADE markers with Tam treatment in LY-treated cultures.

claim: ADE markers (Hhex, Sfrp5, Fzd5) were induced robustly in response to Tam alongside rescue of ADE epithelial morphology even in the presence of LY
source: ADE markers (Hhex, Sfrp5, Fzd5) were induced robustly in response to Tam, alongside the rescue of ADE epithelial morphology, even in the presence of LY (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 5B) and q-RT-PCR data demonstrating marker expression and morphology rescue.

claim: Stimulation of Akt1 by Tam administration rescued the block to ADE induction in both Akt1 expressing and non-expressing cells
source: We found that the stimulation of Akt1 by Tam administration rescued the block to ADE induction in both Akt1 expressing and non-expressing cells (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), indicating cell autonomous and non-autonomous rescue of the LY phenotype.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis of mixed cultures in Figure 5D showing rescue in both GFP+ and GFP- populations.

claim: Akt1 had cell autonomous effects on Snai1 and Sox17 transcription
source: However, based on a time course for induction of gene expression in sorted Akt1-GFP+ and Akt1-GFP− populations (+/− Ly, +/− Tam), it appeared that Akt1 also had cell autonomous effects on Snai1 and Sox17 transcription (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by q-RT-PCR analysis of sorted populations in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A demonstrating differential gene expression responses.

claim: ECM1 but not ECM2 could support ADE differentiation in the presence of LY
source: Figure 6B shows that ECM1, but not ECM2, could support ADE differentiation in the presence of LY.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data in Figure 6B showing ADE formation on ECM1 but not ECM2 in the presence of LY.

claim: ECM1 not only restored anterior induction but the combination of LY and ECM1 enhanced anterior endoderm specification such that cultures were almost 60% ADE
source: Moreover, ECM1 not only restored anterior induction, but the combination of LY and ECM1 enhanced anterior endoderm specification, such that these cultures were almost 60% ADE (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry data in Figure 6B demonstrating high percentage of ADE in ECM1+LY condition.

claim: The capacity of LY to enhance Sox17+Foxa2+ expression was harnessed by ECM1 which converted the Sox17+Foxa2+ naïve population into Hhex+ prospective foregut
source: These data suggest that the capacity of LY to enhance Sox17+Foxa2+ expression was harnessed by ECM1, which was able to convert the Sox17+Foxa2+ naïve population into Hhex+ prospective foregut (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined effects of LY and ECM1 shown in Figure 6B,C demonstrating enhanced ADE formation.

claim: Cells plated on ECM1 in the presence of LY displayed epithelial morphology, enhanced E-cadherin and reduced Snai1 expression
source: Cells plated on ECM1 in the presence of LY displayed epithelial morphology, enhanced E-cadherin and reduced Snai1 expression (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by morphological analysis and q-RT-PCR data in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment of differentiating cultures with LY resulted in loss of expression of tight junction marker ZO-1 and polarity marker aPKC
source: While treatment of differentiating cultures with LY resulted in a loss of expression of the tight junction and polarity markers, ZO-1 and aPKC, organized expression of these was restored within 12 hr of plating onto ECM1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by immunocytochemistry in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C demonstrating loss and restoration of these markers.

claim: Organized expression of ZO-1 and aPKC was restored within 12 hr of plating onto ECM1
source: While treatment of differentiating cultures with LY resulted in a loss of expression of the tight junction and polarity markers, ZO-1 and aPKC, organized expression of these was restored within 12 hr of plating onto ECM1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunocytochemistry in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C showing restoration of marker localization.

claim: Re-plating onto ECM1 did not rescue the LY-mediated block to Akt1 phosphorylation
source: To exclude the possibility that Akt1 activation was somehow stimulated by re-plating on these ECMs, despite the block to PI3K signalling, we assessed Akt1 activation after re-plating and observed no rescue of the LY-mediated block to Akt1 phosphorylation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D showing continued absence of pAkt1 on ECM1 with LY.

claim: ECM1 has the capacity to redirect the LY-mediated enhancement of Sox17/Foxa2 expression through an Akt1 independent pathway
source: Thus, ECM1 has the capacity to redirect the LY-mediated enhancement of Sox17/Foxa2 expression through an Akt1 independent pathway and convert the majority of the culture to properly patterned anterior endoderm.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ECM1 rescues ADE formation without restoring Akt1 phosphorylation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).

claim: ECM1 together with LY could be used to enhance physiological ESC differentiation toward foregut
source: These data suggest that ECM1 together with LY could be used to enhance physiological ESC differentiation toward foregut (Figure 6B, middle panel).
evidence: This is suggested based on the enhanced ADE formation observed with ECM1+LY treatment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Specific proteins enriched in ECM1 include two heparan sulphates proteoglycans (HSPG), Perlecan and Col18a1
source: Specific proteins enriched in ECM1 include two heparan sulphates proteoglycans (HSPG), Perlecan and Col18a1; two HSPG regulators Sulf1 and Cyr61; the metalloprotease Adamts15, the anterior endoderm associated diffusible factors Nodal and Lefty1; and the endoderm/epithelial associated cytokeratines Krt8, Krt18 and Krt19 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 2,3).
evidence: This is based on LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 7A and detailed in source data files.

claim: ECM1 is enriched in HSPG regulators Sulf1 and Cyr61
source: Specific proteins enriched in ECM1 include two heparan sulphates proteoglycans (HSPG), Perlecan and Col18a1; two HSPG regulators Sulf1 and Cyr61; the metalloprotease Adamts15, the anterior endoderm associated diffusible factors Nodal and Lefty1; and the endoderm/epithelial associated cytokeratines Krt8, Krt18 and Krt19 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 2,3).
evidence: This is based on LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 7A and detailed in source data files.

claim: ECM1 is enriched in the metalloprotease Adamts15
source: Specific proteins enriched in ECM1 include two heparan sulphates proteoglycans (HSPG), Perlecan and Col18a1; two HSPG regulators Sulf1 and Cyr61; the metalloprotease Adamts15, the anterior endoderm associated diffusible factors Nodal and Lefty1; and the endoderm/epithelial associated cytokeratines Krt8, Krt18 and Krt19 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 2,3).
evidence: This is based on LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 7A and detailed in source data files.

claim: ECM1 contains the anterior endoderm associated diffusible factors Nodal and Lefty1
source: Specific proteins enriched in ECM1 include two heparan sulphates proteoglycans (HSPG), Perlecan and Col18a1; two HSPG regulators Sulf1 and Cyr61; the metalloprotease Adamts15, the anterior endoderm associated diffusible factors Nodal and Lefty1; and the endoderm/epithelial associated cytokeratines Krt8, Krt18 and Krt19 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 2,3).
evidence: This is based on LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 7A and detailed in source data files.

claim: ECM1 contains the endoderm/epithelial associated cytokeratines Krt8, Krt18 and Krt19
source: Specific proteins enriched in ECM1 include two heparan sulphates proteoglycans (HSPG), Perlecan and Col18a1; two HSPG regulators Sulf1 and Cyr61; the metalloprotease Adamts15, the anterior endoderm associated diffusible factors Nodal and Lefty1; and the endoderm/epithelial associated cytokeratines Krt8, Krt18 and Krt19 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 2,3).
evidence: This is based on LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 7A and detailed in source data files.

claim: Fibronectin (Fn1), a promoter of EMT and migration, was highly enriched in ECM2
source: Interestingly, Fibronectin (Fn1), a promoter of EMT and migration, was highly enriched in ECM2 as was the PS associated diffusible factor Fgf8 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 2,3).
evidence: This is based on LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 7A and detailed in source data files.

claim: The PS associated diffusible factor Fgf8 was highly enriched in ECM2
source: Interestingly, Fibronectin (Fn1), a promoter of EMT and migration, was highly enriched in ECM2 as was the PS associated diffusible factor Fgf8 (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 2,3).
evidence: This is based on LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 7A and detailed in source data files.

claim: Fn1 expression was transcriptionally regulated by PI3K/Akt1 signalling
source: Analysis by q-RT-PCR confirmed that Fn1 expression was transcriptionally regulated by PI3K/Akt1 signalling (Figure 7B), and that the induction of Fn1 expression was a cell autonomous response to Akt1 activation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by q-RT-PCR data in Figure 7B showing differential Fn1 expression with PI3K inhibition.

claim: The induction of Fn1 expression was a cell autonomous response to Akt1 activation
source: Analysis by q-RT-PCR confirmed that Fn1 expression was transcriptionally regulated by PI3K/Akt1 signalling (Figure 7B), and that the induction of Fn1 expression was a cell autonomous response to Akt1 activation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by q-RT-PCR analysis of sorted Akt1-expressing and non-expressing cells in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Addition of Fn1 to differentiating ESC cultures abolished the induction of ADE specific transcription
source: Moreover, the addition of Fn1 to differentiating ESC cultures, either through re-plating of PS stage cultures onto Fn1-coated dishes (data not shown) or through direct addition to phase 2 differentiation (Figure 7C) abolished the induction of ADE specific transcription.
evidence: This is demonstrated by q-RT-PCR data in Figure 7C showing loss of ADE marker expression with Fn1 addition.

claim: Fn1 did not stimulate Akt1 phosphorylation but actually inhibited it
source: Figure 7D shows that Fn1 did not stimulate Akt1 phosphorylation, but it actually inhibited it (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 7D showing reduced pAkt1 levels with Fn1 treatment.

claim: Fn1 was highly expressed in the endoderm of E7.5 embryos
source: Importantly, we found that Fn1 was both highly expressed in the endoderm (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) and robustly enriched in the posterior region of these embryos (Figure 8A,C–E), consistent with a role in promoting naïve endoderm.
evidence: This is shown by q-RT-PCR analysis of dissected embryo regions in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fn1 was robustly enriched in the posterior region of E7.5 embryos
source: Importantly, we found that Fn1 was both highly expressed in the endoderm (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) and robustly enriched in the posterior region of these embryos (Figure 8A,C–E), consistent with a role in promoting naïve endoderm.
evidence: This is demonstrated by q-RT-PCR (Figure 8A) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 8C-E) showing differential Fn1 expression along the A-P axis.

claim: Embryos cultured in the presence of LY exhibit enhanced Fn1 expression
source: Consistent with these observations, immunohistochemistry (IHC) showed that embryos cultured in the presence of LY exhibit enhanced Fn1 expression (Figure 8C,D) and a complete loss of Cer1+ ADE (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in Figure 8C,D showing increased Fn1 staining in LY-treated embryos.

claim: Embryos cultured in the presence of LY show a complete loss of Cer1+ ADE
source: Consistent with these observations, immunohistochemistry (IHC) showed that embryos cultured in the presence of LY exhibit enhanced Fn1 expression (Figure 8C,D) and a complete loss of Cer1+ ADE (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D demonstrating absence of Cer1 expression in LY-treated embryos.

claim: Fn1 protein was non-uniformly distributed along the A-P axis of wild-type E7.5 embryos with relatively low expression in the prospective foregut region where Cer1 was expressed
source: Analysis of wild-type (WT) embryos at E7.5 indicated that Fn1 protein was non-uniformly distributed along the A-P axis, with relatively low expression in the prospective foregut region where Cer1 was expressed (Figure 8A,C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in Figure 8C-E showing inverse correlation between Fn1 and Cer1 expression domains.

claim: In Fn1−/− embryos, the domain of Cer1 expression was expanded toward the posterior-proximal side of the embryo within the domain of Foxa2 expression
source: In Fn1−/− embryos, the domain of Cer1 expression was expanded toward the posterior-proximal side of the embryo within the domain of Foxa2 expression (Figure 8E, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in Figure 8E and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-C showing expanded Cer1 domain in mutant embryos.

claim: Sox17 was expressed at lower levels in the Cer1 positive foregut region
source: We also assessed the protein expression of the pan-endoderm marker Sox17 and found that like Fn1, Sox17 was expressed at lower levels in the Cer1 positive foregut region.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry analysis comparing Sox17 and Cer1 expression patterns.

claim: In Fn1 mutants, the region of Sox17low was expanded across the embryo alongside Cer1
source: In Fn1 mutants, this region of Sox17low was expanded across the embryo alongside Cer1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 3C) and consistent with the increase in Sox17 transcript that we have observed in LY-treated embryos.
evidence: This is shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 8—figure supplement 3C demonstrating expanded Sox17low domain in Fn1 mutants.

claim: Itga5−/− mutant embryos exhibited an expanded domain of Cer1 expression
source: Moreover, while there are a number of integrins that bind to Fn1, integrin Itga5 is thought to mediate Fn1 functions during early embryogenesis and we found that Itga5−/− mutant embryos (Yang et al., 1993) also exhibited an expanded domain of Cer1 expression (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization in Figure 8—figure supplement 2D,E showing expanded Cer1 in Itga5 mutants.

claim: In Fn1 and Itga5 null embryos the foregut did not fold into a tube and remained as a flat field of Foxa2+ cells
source: Consistent with the expansion of Cer1 in these mutants, further foregut morphogenesis was also defective and there was evidence of an expansion in the prospective foregut. In Fn1 and Itga5 null embryos: the foregut did not fold into a tube and remained as a flat field of Foxa2+ cells (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 3B showing foregut morphology defects.

claim: The domain of Foxa2+ cells remained enlarged in Fn1 and Itga5 null embryos compared to control embryos, particularly apparent early in foregut morphogenesis (E7.75)
source: This domain of Foxa2+ cells remained enlarged compared to control embryos and this was particularly apparent early in foregut morphogenesis (E7.75) (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is shown by in situ hybridization in Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 3A,B demonstrating expanded Foxa2 domain.

claim: FGF signalling has been linked to visceral endoderm-dependent deposition of basement membrane components in ESC differentiation
source: For example, PS formation can be inhibited on the anterior side of the embryo as a consequence of the visceral endoderm depositing ECM components that block cell migration (Egea et al., 2008) and FGF signalling has been linked to visceral endoderm-dependent deposition of basement membrane components in ESC differentiation (Villegas et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Villegas et al., 2010).

claim: PS formation can be inhibited on the anterior side of the embryo as a consequence of the visceral endoderm depositing ECM components that block cell migration
source: For example, PS formation can be inhibited on the anterior side of the embryo as a consequence of the visceral endoderm depositing ECM components that block cell migration (Egea et al., 2008) and FGF signalling has been linked to visceral endoderm-dependent deposition of basement membrane components in ESC differentiation (Villegas et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Egea et al., 2008).

claim: Integrin Itga5 is thought to mediate Fn1 functions during early embryogenesis
source: Moreover, while there are a number of integrins that bind to Fn1, integrin Itga5 is thought to mediate Fn1 functions during early embryogenesis and we found that Itga5−/− mutant embryos (Yang et al., 1993) also exhibited an expanded domain of Cer1 expression (Figure 8—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field and supported by citation.

claim: Fn1-integrin interactions are essential for axial extension of the mesendoderm
source: Genetic studies indicate that Fn1-integrin interactions are essential for axial extension of the mesendoderm (Yang et al., 1999; Davidson et al., 2006; Marsden and DeSimone, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple genetic studies.

claim: Fn1 is not required for gastrulation
source: However, Fn1 is not required for gastrulation and specific endodermal patterning defects have not been previously reported.
evidence: This is stated based on existing knowledge from the literature.

claim: The Fn1 and Itga5 null mutants are both embryonic lethal and die by E10.5 due to cardiovascular problems, posterior truncations, and kinking of the neural tube
source: The Fn1 and Itga5 null mutants are both embryonic lethal and die by E10.5 due to cardiovascular problems, posterior truncations, and kinking of the neural tube among others defects (George et al., 1993; Yang et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: PI3K/Akt1 signalling has been extensively associated with the induction of EMT rather than its suppression
source: PI3K/Akt1 signalling has been extensively associated with the induction of EMT (Larue and Bellacosa, 2005) rather than its suppression.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field supported by citation.

claim: FGF receptor activation is essential for ESC differentiation towards multiple lineages and leads to Grb2 and SHP2 recruitment, activating both PI3K and MAPK signalling pathways
source: FGF receptor activation is essential for ESC differentiation towards multiple lineages and leads to Grb2 and SHP2 recruitment, activating both PI3K and MAPK signalling pathways (Kouhara et al., 1997; Xu et al., 1998; Villegas et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on FGF signaling.

claim: MAPK pathways have been associated with mesoderm induction, EMT and cell migration during gastrulation
source: These pathways have been associated with mesoderm induction, EMT and cell migration during gastrulation (Casey et al., 1998; Rodaway et al., 1999; Ciruna and Rossant, 2001; Mizoguchi et al., 2006; Poulain et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: In endoderm, FGF signalling is required but does not induce EMT
source: In endoderm, where FGF signalling is required, but does not induce EMT (Morrison et al., 2008; Hansson et al., 2009), the signalling is contextualized and rendered distinct as a result of the activity of this pathway in remodelling the ECM.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on FGF signaling in endoderm.

claim: PI3K activity in the visceral endoderm of embryoid body differentiation has been associated with the production of ECM required to support the epithelialization of the epiblast
source: PI3K activity in the visceral endoderm of embryoid body differentiation (Li et al., 2001) has also been associated with the production of ECM required to support the epithelialization of the epiblast (Jeanes et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of PI3K/Akt1 pathway has been associated with a block to EMT in human ESCs
source: While the activity of PI3K/Akt1 is generally associated with induction of EMT, activation of this pathway has also been associated with a block to EMT in human ESCs (Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study on human ESCs.

claim: In human ESCs, Akt1 activation supports self-renewal by inhibiting Raf/Mek/Erk and canonical Wnt signalling
source: In this context, Akt1 activation supports human ESC self-renewal by inhibiting Raf/Mek/Erk and canonical Wnt signalling, which in turn may also promote EMT, although it is not clear whether this route takes place in vivo during early endoderm differentiation or how comparable the mouse and human ESC differentiation models are.
evidence: This claim is based on previous work cited (Singh et al., 2012) but with caveats about applicability.

claim: Knock down of Perlecan and Col18a1 HSPGs impairs endoderm differentiation in vitro
source: Knock down of these two HSPG's have been shown to impair endoderm differentiation in vitro (Higuchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Specific modifications in the ECM are required for Nodal transport within the embryo
source: It has been suggested that specific modifications in the ECM are required for Nodal transport within the embryo (Oki et al., 2007; Marjoram and Wright, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Nodal signaling.

claim: Inhibition of PI3K leads to enhanced Sox17 and Foxa2 expression
source: The observation that inhibition of PI3K leads to enhanced Sox17 and Foxa2 expression (McLean et al., 2007) has been used in ESC differentiation protocols to generate endoderm derivatives.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.
